title: Deep-frying oil records: when to change the oil and what to write down
excerpt: The limit for polar compounds in food service is 24%: once it is reached, change the oil, no matter how it looks. Learn what to record in the replacement log and how to dispose of fryer oil.

body.text: Frying fat is one of the kitchen’s most deceptive ingredients. It may still look usable, while chemically it has turned into a mixture of acrylamides and aldehydes. That is why the rule is to measure it rather than judge it by appearance: usually once per shift, and more often when frying is intensive.

The key indicator is the percentage of polar compounds. The limit in food service is 24%. Once it reaches that level, change the oil regardless of whether it “still fries well.” Measure it with a handheld analyzer or test strips.
What to record in the journal

items: Measurement result as a percentage of polar compounds.
Action: continue using the oil or replace it.
When replacing it, record the volume and disposal method (including the separate collection contract).

body.title: Disposal is mandatory
body.text: Pouring fryer oil into the sewer is a direct violation of sanitary rules and the agreement with the water utility. Used oil must be collected in a separate container and removed under a collection report.

The template fills in typical values, reminds you to measure at the start of a shift, and automatically marks a result in red if it exceeds 24%. The disposal report is attached to the replacement entry, so an inspector can immediately see the complete process.
